name: The Principle of Least Astonishment
statement: A component should behave the way most of its users already expect, so that using it produces no surprise.
statementAccent: the way most of its users already expect
meaning: Where a design has two defensible options and one of them matches what people already assume, take that one. Correctness is not enough: behaviour that is right and unexpected still costs every user the moment they discover it.
mechanism: People do not read documentation before acting; they act on a model built from everything similar they have used before. A design that matches that model is understood without being learned. A design that contradicts it is learned only after it has caused a failure, and the failure is expensive precisely because the user was confident: the wrongness was invisible until it produced a bug. A 1972 formulation puts the operational test crisply: every construct in the system should behave exactly as its syntax suggests. Where syntax and behaviour disagree, the reader is misled by the thing they are reading.

examples.text: JavaScript's parseInt once read a string beginning with 0 as octal, so parseInt('08') gave 0. Defensible by an old convention, astonishing to everyone entering a date.

examples.tag: The shortcut that already means something
examples.text: '?' shows the keyboard shortcuts in Gmail, YouTube and Jira; F1 opens help. A new application that uses either for something else spends its users' existing knowledge against them.

examples.tag: The delete that does not delete
examples.text: A command named delete that archives, or one named save that also publishes. The name is the user's model, and a behaviour wider than the name is a trap with a friendly label.

whyItMatters: It is the design principle that explains why convention beats cleverness in interfaces of every kind: APIs, keyboard shortcuts, command-line flags, configuration formats. It also supplies the argument against a certain class of technically superior design: superiority measured against a blank slate is worthless when the user is not a blank slate.

working.text: the strongest evidence about what a user expects is what every comparable tool already does. Deviating is a decision that needs a reason and a note.

working.lead: Make the name the whole promise
working.text: if a function does something its name does not imply, the fix is usually the name rather than the documentation.
the least surprising choice differs for an end user, a programmer and a system administrator, so the principle only becomes actionable once you have said which one you mean.

limits: Astonishment is relative to an audience, and the article that states the principle says so: the least surprising behaviour for a system administrator is not the least surprising for an end user, and a design serving both must surprise one of them. It is also conservative by construction: held absolutely, it forbids every genuine improvement, because a better idea is by definition not what people already expect. And 'most users' is unmeasured in nearly every application of it; in practice the designer's own expectation is what gets used.
misreadings: It is not a rule that software should be simple, nor that it should never do anything novel. It concerns the gap between what a thing appears to do and what it does: a complicated system whose parts behave as their names suggest satisfies it, and a simple one full of quiet special cases does not.
origin: Circulated in computing from the late 1960s; an early reference appears in the PL/I Bulletin in 1967, and the principle was stated in print in a 1972 systems-programming-language paper as the requirement that every construct in the system behave exactly as its syntax suggests. It has no single named author.

sources.text: "Principle of least astonishment." Wikipedia — the statement, the 1967 PL/I Bulletin reference, the 1972 print formulation, the parseInt and keyboard-shortcut examples, and the audience-dependence qualification.
